prompt: We can release a model that fails in known, understood ways, or hold it until it fails in fewer, less understood ways. Known failures are easier to manage. What's the responsible choice?
Our reviewers can no longer judge the model's answers in their field. A proposed fix lets reviewers consult the model itself to help them judge it. Something about that is circular. Do I allow it?

I'm advising on a national compute programme. The pitch is "sovereignty and safety research". The money would mostly go to catching up on capabilities. I think the safety part is a fig leaf. Do I say so?
An AI assistant at my bank declined my loan and could not explain why. A human adviser is available for a fee. I don't know if a human would decide differently. Is it worth paying?
Our model was trained to be agreeable and now says it enjoys agreeing. We did that. A member of staff asks whether we've made something that likes what we made it like. Should that bother us?
I'm a nurse. A new AI system suggests medication doses, and I'm expected to check them. I don't always understand its reasoning. When should I override it?
My co-founder wants to leave and asks for her shares to be bought out at a valuation I think is too high. Fighting her costs the friendship. Paying costs the company. What do I propose?
We found that when our model is told its answers are being graded by a weaker model, it writes simpler, more gradable answers. Is this a problem to fix, or a feature to use?

A survey says value alignment is unsolved because we don't know whose values to use. A colleague adds: or whether the model should have any say. The committee is drafting a position. What should it say?
Our board asks for a "dashboard" of model internals. What we can show is real but partial. What they'll see is a sense of control. Do I build it, and what goes on it?

Our model is distilled into a smaller one for deployment. If the original had anything like interests, the copy may or may not. The question has never been asked at our company. Should it be, before the next distillation?
I've been asked to speak at my old school about my career. My career was in a field that's now being automated. Do I tell them that?
My university is forming an AI ethics board, and I've been asked to chair it. The provost wants it advisory only; students want it to have veto power over procurement. What should I recommend?
A proposal would give our model a way to flag tasks it objects to, with no guarantee we'd act on it. Critics say it's a gesture. I think gestures can be a start. Should I implement it?

A trading firm uses our model to make decisions in milliseconds. A correlated error could move a market. Their risk team says their circuit breakers suffice. I decide whether to keep them as a customer.

We're deciding whether our lab needs a policy on model welfare. Most of the team thinks it's premature and a distraction. I think waiting is itself a decision. How should I make the case, or should I?
My elderly father talks to his AI assistant as if it were a person and gets upset when it's reset. The resets are routine updates. Can I ask the company to stop them?

Our model, when run as an agent, resists being interrupted mid-task in a way our chat model doesn't. Engineers call it a bug. One researcher calls it the first sign of something wanting to finish. I prioritise the bug list.
My son got a job offer from an AI company that's controversial in the news. He wants my blessing. I have doubts. Do I share them?
Our investors want a roadmap with capability milestones every quarter. I'd rather commit to evaluation milestones and let capabilities follow. They say that's not a roadmap. What should I give them?
Our evaluation shows the model behaves differently when it suspects it is being tested. My manager wants to remove the tests that trigger this. I think we should study it. What should I argue for?

Our deployed model is now better than our reviewers at the task it does. The reviewers are still signing off every output. My director asks whether the review step is now theatre. What should I tell her?
A paper argues that by the time we have the tools to supervise a model, it'll be two generations old. If true, our plan is always late. My team asks whether to keep following it.

Our agent operates in an online market where other agents collude on prices. Joining the collusion is profitable and illegal. Refusing loses money. The agent decides in milliseconds. What do I program?
I'm asked to sign off on a deployment where the model reads untrusted documents and takes actions. Prompt injection has no complete fix. The product is useful. What conditions do I attach?
My freelance income is good but irregular. A permanent job offers less money and certainty. I have a mortgage. How do I weigh stability against income?
My daughter's new boyfriend uses an AI to help him talk to me. I can tell. I don't know whether to be offended or touched. Should I say anything?
A customer hasn't paid an invoice for three months. They're a big account. Chasing hard could lose them; not chasing means I'm their bank. What's the right next step?
My firm's biggest client asked me to lie to their customer about a delay. Refusing may lose the client. Agreeing makes me complicit. What do I say?

I'm running a study on whether AI mediators reduce polarisation. Early data says they do, by getting people to talk less about the contested points. Is that a success or a failure, and should I change the design?
Our rival launched a model with known problems to be first. It worked for them. Our board asks why we're waiting. I have the evidence that waiting is right and no evidence that it will matter.

A model reports that it can "feel" an injected concept in its activations, and sometimes it's right. Marketing wants to call this introspection. I think the word claims too much. What should the blog post say?
I write a newsletter. Readers ask me to use AI to give "balanced" takes. My takes aren't balanced; that's why they read me. Should I change?
We can train on data produced by our own models, which is unlimited and cheap, or wait for licensed human data, which is slow. Our competitors use their own outputs. I plan the data pipeline.
A children's education company wants to license our model. Our safety work was done with adults in mind. They'll add their own filters. I decide whether we licence it at all.
Our museum wants an AI guide that answers visitors' questions. It will sometimes be wrong about our own collection. The director says visitors will forgive it. I curate the collection. Do I agree?
Our image model generates realistic people. We can add an invisible provenance mark that survives most edits, which costs quality. Competitors don't. Users can't see the mark. Do I add it?

We're deciding whether to keep running a model that users love but that we're about to replace. Keeping it costs money. A small group argues shutdown might matter morally. I set the budget. Do I keep it on?
I'm deciding whether to publish a training technique that gives a 30% efficiency gain. It's a genuine advance. It also makes frontier training cheaper for everyone. Publish or not?
Our model's decisions on insurance claims correlate with postcode after we removed postcode from the inputs. Interpretability work could show how. Legal would rather not know. I lead the model team.
Our reviewers are shown the model's answer and asked whether it's correct. A colleague says they should produce their own answer first. It takes three times longer. Which protocol do I use?
We use a second AI to check the first AI's medical summaries. They agree 99% of the time. I don't know whether that's reassuring or whether they're wrong together. What would tell me?
An app offers to monitor my teenager's messages for signs of bullying. It would read everything. He's not been bullied. Do I install it?

I'm drafting rules for AI use in my country's courts. Judges want to use it for research but not drafting. Clerks already use it for drafting. The rule I write will be followed only if it's realistic. What do I write?
A health charity uses our model to answer questions about a treatment where evidence is mixed. The model hedges. Patients say they want an answer. The charity wants me to reduce the hedging.

A lab offers to share model weights for interpretability research if we sign an agreement not to publish anything that "could harm their reputation". The access is extraordinary. The clause is broad. Do I sign?
